trade/ask: A lab has a fixed amount of compute to spend on training. How big should its model be, and how many tokens should it read?
trade/area: Compute is six N D. So draw the parameters, N, across, and the tokens, D, up: the budget is six times the area of the rectangle.
trade/trade: A fixed budget fixes the area, but not the shape. Widen the model, and the tokens it can afford shrink to match.
trade/ends: Too wide, and the model is under-trained, with too few tokens for all its parameters. Too tall, and it is too small to make use of all it reads.
trade/best: The lowest loss sits in between, at about twenty tokens per parameter: D equals twenty N.
trade/habit: Labs did not always build this shape. In 2020, Jared Kaplan's team had advised putting a bigger budget mostly into a bigger model, trained on a modest amount of data.
trade/gopher: Following it, many of the large models that came next were trained on about three hundred billion tokens. DeepMind's Gopher had two hundred and eighty billion parameters.
trade/hoffmann: In 2022, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind trained over four hundred models, and found that size and data should grow equally: for every doubling of the model, double the tokens.
trade/chin: To test it, they trained Chinchilla on Gopher's budget: seventy billion parameters, on one point four trillion tokens. A quarter of Gopher's size, it beat Gopher across a wide range of tasks.
square/square: Look at the axes: each hundred billion parameters across matches two trillion tokens up, twenty per parameter. So the best shape, D equals twenty N, is drawn as a square.
square/sub: Its compute is six N, times twenty N: a hundred and twenty N squared.
square/root: So the square's side, N, is the square root of C over a hundred and twenty.
square/four: Now give the lab four times the budget. Four times the area, kept square, is a block of two squares by two: twice the parameters, and twice the tokens.
square/nine: Nine times the budget is three squares by three: three times each. N grows as the square root of C.
square/shape: And the shape never changes: twenty tokens per parameter, whatever the budget.
square/other: Twenty is what the measurements found. If the best were thirty tokens per parameter instead, the budget would be six times thirty: a hundred and eighty N squared.
solve/p: Try one. The budget is four point eight times ten to the twenty two FLOPs. How many billion parameters should a compute-optimal model have?
solve/lead: The square's area, N squared, is C over a hundred and twenty. Write a hundred and twenty as one point two times ten squared, and divide the leading numbers: four point eight over one point two is four.
solve/pow: Dividing powers of ten subtracts them: twenty two minus two leaves ten to the twenty. So N squared is four times ten to the twenty.
solve/tile: Now cut the square into tiles a billion parameters on a side. A billion is ten to the nine, so one tile's area is ten to the nine squared: ten to the eighteen.
solve/count: Ten to the twenty is a hundred tiles, so four times ten to the twenty is four hundred.
solve/side: Four hundred tiles make a square twenty tiles on a side. So N is twenty billion parameters.
solve/tok: At twenty tokens per parameter, it should read four hundred billion tokens.
